name: Zoe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at a big warehouse-style supermarket on the edge of town, where people shop in bulk. I run a section of six tills, handle returns and train the weekend staff. I like the volume, it makes the shift fly, and the regulars who come in with trolleys full. What wears me out is the long rows of customers on Saturdays and being on the phone to head office about stock. I sing in the church choir on Sundays, which is how I recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a flash in the pan. I'd tell the team to keep doing a good job and not worry. At church I wouldn't bring it up, there are better things to talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm calm about it. We'd get some new tools and some old jobs would shift, but the place needs good people. If the routine stuff is automated, I'd have more time with customers, which is what I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and save 200 a month towards my dream, which is a small bakery-and-deli shop. I'd try the AI for inventory notes, as I do now. And I'd keep praying and singing, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a little worry about rent. Nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your money plans: what is the goal you're saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to open a small deli with homemade bread in a few years, and my partner Caleb, who fixes farm machinery, would help with the fit-out. We're saving for a deposit on a unit. I've got about three months in the bank, which isn't a lot for a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your church friends say about AI in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say it's a test of how we treat each other, probably. We'd talk about who gets left out. Our pastor is often on about caring for people who lose their jobs.

say: It's a bit of a **flash in the pan**, so keep doing a good job.
At church I wouldn't bring it up; there are **better things** to talk about.
think: I'm calm: the place needs **good people**.
If routine work is automated, I'd get more **time with customers**, which I like.
do: Save **200 a month** towards a small bakery-and-deli.
feel: Fairly **settled**, with a little worry about rent.
S0.quote: If the routine stuff is automated, I'd have more time with customers, which is what I like.
fieldNote: Her **dream shop** gives her a reason to save and a view of work beyond the till.
Faith and the choir are how she recovers.
Three months saved is thin for starting a business.

steps.text: Save 200 a month towards a bakery-and-deli deposit
Use AI to draft inventory notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, and we should help people through it. I'd tell the team to learn the tools and not be afraid. At church I'd offer to run a small class on basic computer skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering, stock counts and returns paperwork would go to software. That's what makes me team lead and not just a cashier. The checkouts and the customers' questions are still done by people, mostly, but we have more self-service every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any training the company offers, and I'd also do an online course in running a small food business. I'd ask head office for more hours on the planning side. I'd put 250 a month away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, not afraid. It feels like the weather turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your section would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it more urgent. If I wait too long my job might not exist, but if I jump too early I'd lose my cushion. I'd say within two years I'd start with a market stall on Saturdays, to test the bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change your shop plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deli plan stays and grows. Software could actually help me, with ordering and bookkeeping. I'd say it's an advantage for the small shop, if I learn it.

I'd offer a small **computer skills class** at church.

fieldNote: Reads software as both a **threat** to her team-lead role and a tool for her future shop.
Plans a Saturday market stall to test the bread within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should look after each other and also be honest. At church I'd ask people to check on their neighbours. At work I'd say we should all learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's really serious. By 2028 the thinking jobs go, including a lot of the planning in my head office, and by 2031 the robots do the tills and the stacking. My team-lead job goes at the same time as the ordinary cashiers. I'd have to build something that machines can't, like a shop with a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd try to launch the stall quickly and see if there's demand. I'd cut costs, pause the deposit plan but keep the savings. I'd ask Caleb to help with the stall. And I'd learn the AI tools properly, as they could help me run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit hurried. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your bakery plan in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery plan becomes the main plan, and I'd go faster. A deli in a town where people have lost jobs may be tough. But a good loaf and a kind face matter even more then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the weekend staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them honestly that the next few years will be hard and to keep their savings. I'd show them how I'm learning and tell them to look for something they can build themselves. I'd say we'd get through it together.

say: We should **look after each other** and also be honest.
At church I'd ask people to **check on neighbours**.

My team-lead role goes at the same time as the **cashiers**.

feel: **Anxious** and hurried; I'd pray more and sleep less.

fieldNote: Her dream becomes the **main plan**, brought forward by fear.
Sees her team-lead role as just as exposed as the cashiers'.

steps.text: Launch the Saturday bread stall within three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, but only if we start. At church I'd talk about looking after those who'll be hit hardest. At work I'd say learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hopeful, but still anxious. I'd be 32 in 2031 and the robots come around 2034. That gives me time to get the shop going and keep the supermarket wage while I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the stall this spring, save 300 a month, and open a small unit in year three. I'd do a bookkeeping course and use AI for the admin. I'd keep my team-lead job until the shop supports me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with hope in it. Having a plan helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, is the shop plan safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit safer, but the supermarket job might be gone around 2034, so the shop has to be running by then. I'd rather not run the shop with no cushion. Three months isn't enough, so I'd aim for six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to Caleb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's do the stall now, the unit in three years and the wedding after. Caleb says he'd rather wait for the shop than marry on a shoestring. So we've agreed on that order.

At church I'd talk about looking after those **hit hardest**.

I'd keep the supermarket **wage** while I build.

feel: **Anxious**, with hope in it, because a plan helps.
S3.quote: I'd rather not run the shop with no cushion. Three months isn't enough, so I'd aim for six.
fieldNote: Wants a **six-month cushion** before running a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it to help each other. At church I'd start a skills group. At work I'd train juniors to take over from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I suppose. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots in 2039. By then I'd want to have a business running that machines can't easily do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the deli in about four years, once I've saved 12,000. I'd do a food-business course and use AI for the bookkeeping. I'd marry Caleb in year three, and we'd think about kids. I'd keep my choir and my faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. There's still a worry that the dream won't make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deli that's busy on Saturdays, Caleb fixing machines nearby, and a few young people working for me whom I've trained. I'd like to give people the kind of start I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good result look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little tension, but not much. I'd keep the supermarket job for security until the deli pays, which might take two years.

I'd start a **skills group** at church and train juniors at work.

I want a business that machines can't easily do.

fieldNote: Time lets her **sequence** shop, wedding and family without panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. There's no time to get the shop running and I'd still have only three months saved. What would help is a small-business loan with fair terms, training on the AI tools for bookkeeping, and local people who still buy from local shops. I'd also like churches and councils to help people who are hit first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stuck in the past. We love tradition, but we also want to build something. What we want is the freedom to try it ourselves.

headlineQuote: What we want is the freedom to try it ourselves.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old **team lead** at a warehouse-style supermarket, running six tills and training weekend staff.
She is traditional, sings in her church choir and dreams of opening a small bakery-and-deli.
She uses AI tools now and then and lives with Caleb, a farm-machinery mechanic, with about three months saved.
Her answer to each scenario is to bring the **shop** forward or slow it, depending on the time.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because she'd have no time to get the shop going with three months saved.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **small-business loan**, training on AI for bookkeeping, and local customers who stay loyal.
